title: Judging performance: alpha, tracking error, overlap, rebalancing, Rule of 72
objectives: Explain alpha, tracking error and portfolio overlap in one sentence each.
Say when rebalancing is due and how the Rule of 72 estimates doubling time.
body_md:
Alpha is return above what the benchmark (adjusted for risk) delivered. Tracking error shows how closely an index fund follows its index; lower is better. Portfolio overlap shows how much two funds hold the same stocks — two large-cap funds with 70% overlap add little diversification. Portfolio turnover is how often the manager buys and sells; high turnover means higher hidden trading costs. Rebalancing brings the asset mix back to target after markets move it. A fund should be judged against its TRI over 3–5 years, not one year. The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time: 72 ÷ yearly return = years to double.

| Term | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alpha | Return above what the benchmark (adjusted for risk) delivered | Fund 14%, benchmark 12% → roughly 2% alpha |
| Tracking error | How closely an index fund follows its index; lower is better | 0.05% vs 0.5% tracking error |
| Portfolio overlap | How much two funds hold the same stocks | Two large-cap funds with 70% overlap add little diversification |
| Portfolio turnover | How often the fund manager buys and sells; high turnover means higher hidden trading costs | Turnover 30% vs 150% |
| Rebalancing | Bringing the asset mix back to target after markets move it | 60:40 drifted to 72:28 → move some gains back to debt |
| Benchmark-beating | Fund return after costs compared with TRI over 3–5 years, not one year | One bad year is not a reason to exit |
| Rule of 72 | Quick estimate: 72 ÷ yearly return = years to double | At 12%, money doubles in about 6 years |

> **Investor takeaway:** Compare like with like: XIRR for SIPs, CAGR for lump sums, against the TRI benchmark, over at least 3–5 years.
example: At 12% a year, money doubles in about 6 years by the Rule of 72; a 60:40 mix drifted to 72:28 is rebalanced by moving some gains back to debt.
say: One bad year is not a reason to exit a fund.
Compare a fund with its TRI over 3–5 years, not one year.
never: A fund that beat its benchmark last year is proven better.
Rebalancing means chasing the best-performing asset.
